families.name: Rehearsal-Based Methods
families.definition: These methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing or generating a subset of past data to replay during the training of new tasks.

properties.text: They maintain performance on previous tasks by mixing old and new data in the training batch.
They are generally easy to implement and integrate with standard deep learning pipelines.
They are effective when a small, representative subset of past data is sufficient to retain knowledge.
They apply well in scenarios where data storage is feasible and privacy constraints allow for data retention.

limitations.text: They face significant storage constraints as the number of tasks and data points grows over time.
They are vulnerable to privacy and legal issues regarding the retention of personal smart city data.
They suffer from representational bias if the stored subset does not adequately cover the distribution of past tasks.
They become computationally expensive if large amounts of data must be replayed frequently.

families.name: Regularization-Based Methods
families.definition: These approaches constrain the model's weight updates to prevent significant changes to parameters that are critical for previously learned tasks.

properties.text: They do not require storing any past data, making them memory-efficient.
They work by adding penalty terms to the loss function that measure the importance of weights.
They are suitable for scenarios with strict privacy requirements where data retention is prohibited.
They are particularly effective when the model architecture remains fixed across tasks.

limitations.text: They often struggle with high task similarity, where important weights for different tasks overlap.
They can lead to underfitting on new tasks due to excessive regularization.
They are sensitive to the estimation of weight importance, which can be inaccurate in dynamic smart city environments.
They generally perform worse than rehearsal-based methods when the number of tasks is large.

families.name: Architecture-Based Methods
families.definition: These techniques modify the neural network structure to isolate knowledge for different tasks, such as through dynamic expansion or parameter isolation.

properties.text: They prevent interference by allocating separate parameters or sub-networks for each task.
They allow for the addition of new modules as new tasks emerge without retraining the entire model.
They are highly effective for scenarios with distinct, non-overlapping task domains.
They support efficient inference by routing inputs to the specific module trained for that task.

limitations.text: They suffer from model size explosion as the number of tasks increases.
They require a mechanism to identify which task an input belongs to, which can be ambiguous in smart cities.
They do not share knowledge across tasks, potentially missing generalizable patterns.
They are less effective when tasks are highly related and could benefit from shared representations.

families.name: Prompt-Based Methods
families.definition: These methods learn task-specific prompts or adapters that condition a frozen or partially frozen backbone model to perform different tasks.

properties.text: They leverage pre-trained foundation models, reducing the need for extensive retraining.
They are parameter-efficient, as only the small prompt vectors or adapter modules are updated.
They are well-suited for smart city applications where large pre-trained models are available.
They allow for rapid adaptation to new tasks by learning new prompts without altering the core model.

limitations.text: They depend heavily on the quality and generalizability of the pre-trained backbone.
They may struggle with tasks that are fundamentally different from the pre-training distribution.
They require careful management of prompt storage and retrieval for many tasks.
They can suffer from prompt interference if prompts are not sufficiently distinct.
